Gaussian Discriminant Analysis
& Maximum Likelihood Estimation

From probability distributions to decision boundaries — deriving classifiers through risk minimization and fitting them to data via likelihood maximization.

Learning Objectives

  • State the generative model underlying Gaussian Discriminant Analysis and write the class-conditional PDF for $d$-dimensional data with scalar variance.
  • Derive the quadratic discriminant function $q_c(\mathbf{x})$ from the Bayes decision rule by taking the log-posterior, and explain why the resulting decision function is quadratic in $\mathbf{x}$.
  • Apply QDA to a two-class problem: compute $q_c(\mathbf{x}) - q_d(\mathbf{x})$, identify the decision boundary, and classify new points.
  • Identify the additional assumption that transforms QDA into LDA, derive the resulting linear decision function, and explain the geometric meaning of the weight vector.
  • Recognize the logistic (sigmoid) function as the natural output of Gaussian discriminant analysis and interpret its value as a posterior probability.
  • Extend GDA to more than two classes using the argmax of per-class discriminant functions, and describe the resulting multi-class decision regions.
  • Define the likelihood function and the log-likelihood, and formulate maximum likelihood estimation as an optimization problem.
  • Derive the MLE for the parameters of a Gaussian distribution — the sample mean and (biased) sample variance — and explain the bias of the MLE variance estimator.

7.1 The Generative Model: Class-Conditional Gaussians

The classifiers we have studied so far — support vector machines, nearest-neighbor methods, and the centroid classifier — are discriminative in spirit: they draw a boundary between classes without explicitly modeling how the data within each class was generated. A different and deeply illuminating perspective asks: what probability distribution gave rise to the observed data? If we can answer that question for each class separately, then classifying a new point becomes a question about which class's distribution most plausibly generated it. This is the generative approach to classification.

Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (GDA) is the canonical generative classifier. Its central assumption is simple and often remarkably accurate: the data points belonging to each class are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian (normal) distribution. Each class has its own mean and its own spread, and together these distributions, combined with prior probabilities for each class, completely specify the probabilistic model. Once we have this model, the Bayes decision rule — always predict the class with the highest posterior probability — leads naturally to a concrete, computable classifier.

In this section we establish the mathematical foundation: the form of the Gaussian distribution we will use, and how prior probabilities and class-conditional densities combine to produce posterior probabilities.

7.1.1 The Multivariate Gaussian with Scalar Variance

The general multivariate Gaussian in $d$ dimensions has a $d \times d$ covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$. While powerful, this generality introduces $O(d^2)$ parameters and can lead to overfitting when training data is limited. As a first simplification — which we relax in Section 7.4 and in later chapters — we assume that the covariance matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity: $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$. This makes the distribution isotropic: its spread is the same in every direction, so its iso-probability contours are spheres rather than ellipsoids.

Definition · Isotropic Multivariate Gaussian

A random vector $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ follows an isotropic multivariate Gaussian distribution with mean $\boldsymbol\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and scalar variance $\sigma^2 > 0$, written $\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I})$, if its probability density function is $$f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{d/2}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \quad \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d.$$ Here $\|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^d (x_j - \mu_j)^2$ is the squared Euclidean distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\boldsymbol\mu$, and $d$ is the dimension of the feature space.

A few features of this density are worth noting. The normalizing constant $(2\pi\sigma^2)^{d/2}$ is purely a function of $d$ and $\sigma^2$; it does not depend on $\mathbf{x}$ or $\boldsymbol\mu$. The density achieves its maximum at $\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol\mu$, and decays monotonically as we move away from $\boldsymbol\mu$. Crucially, the decay depends only on the Euclidean distance from $\boldsymbol\mu$, so all points at the same distance from the mean have equal density — hence the spherical iso-contours.

Intuition · Why Scalar Variance Produces Spherical Contours

Think of $\sigma$ as the "radius" of the Gaussian. When $\sigma$ is the same in every coordinate direction, moving one unit along $x_1$ decreases the density by exactly the same factor as moving one unit along $x_2$, $x_3$, or any other direction. The set of points at which the density equals some constant $k$ is therefore the set $\{\mathbf{x} : \|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu\| = r\}$ for some radius $r$ — a sphere centered at $\boldsymbol\mu$. A full covariance matrix, by contrast, stretches and rotates these spheres into ellipsoids, allowing the distribution to be narrow in some directions and wide in others.

7.1.2 Class-Conditional Distributions and Priors

In a classification problem with $K$ classes (labeled $c = 1, \ldots, K$), the GDA model assigns each class its own Gaussian. The distribution of feature vectors belonging to class $c$ is

$$\mathbf{X} \mid Y = c \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu_c, \sigma_c^2 \mathbf{I}),$$

where $\boldsymbol\mu_c \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the mean of class $c$ and $\sigma_c^2 > 0$ is its variance. We write the corresponding class-conditional PDF as $f_{\mathbf{X}|Y=c}(\mathbf{x})$. In addition, each class has a prior probability $\pi_c = \mathbb{P}(Y = c)$, which captures how often class $c$ appears in the population regardless of the feature value. The priors must satisfy $\sum_{c=1}^K \pi_c = 1$.

Definition · GDA Generative Model

The Gaussian Discriminant Analysis model for $K$ classes specifies, for each class $c \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$:

  • A prior probability $\pi_c = \mathbb{P}(Y = c) > 0$ with $\sum_c \pi_c = 1$.
  • A class-conditional PDF $f_c(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq f_{\mathbf{X}|Y=c}(\mathbf{x}) = \dfrac{1}{(2\pi\sigma_c^2)^{d/2}} \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2}{2\sigma_c^2}\right).$
The joint density of $(\mathbf{X}, Y)$ is $f(\mathbf{x}, c) = \pi_c \, f_c(\mathbf{x})$, and by Bayes' theorem the posterior probability of class $c$ given observation $\mathbf{x}$ is $$\mathbb{P}(Y = c \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\pi_c \, f_c(\mathbf{x})}{\sum_{c'=1}^K \pi_{c'} f_{c'}(\mathbf{x})}.$$

The denominator $f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{c'} \pi_{c'} f_{c'}(\mathbf{x})$ is the marginal density of $\mathbf{X}$ — the overall density of the data averaged over all classes. For prediction, however, we never need to compute it: since it is the same for all classes, maximizing the numerator $\pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x})$ over $c$ is equivalent to maximizing the posterior.

Figure 7.1. Left: One-dimensional class-conditional PDFs weighted by their priors, $\pi_C f_C(x)$ (blue) and $\pi_D f_D(x)$ (red), with $\mu_C = 1$, $\sigma_C = 1.2$, $\pi_C = 0.55$ and $\mu_D = 5.5$, $\sigma_D = 1.6$, $\pi_D = 0.45$. The golden dashed vertical line marks the Bayes decision boundary — the point where both weighted densities are equal. A test point to the left of the boundary is classified as $C$; to the right as $D$. Right: Iso-contours of the same two distributions in 2D, showing spherical (isotropic) level sets. The golden curve is the QDA decision boundary.
💡
Key insight: The GDA model is generative — it specifies a full probability model over inputs and labels. This is in contrast to discriminative models like SVMs, which directly model the boundary without describing the data distribution within each class.

7.2 Quadratic Discriminant Analysis

We now derive the concrete classification rule that emerges from the GDA model. The Bayes decision rule says: given a test point $\mathbf{x}$, predict the class $c^*$ that maximizes the posterior probability $\mathbb{P}(Y = c \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})$. As argued above, this is equivalent to maximizing the numerator $\pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x})$ over all classes $c$. While correct, this expression involves an exponential function of $\mathbf{x}$, which can be numerically inconvenient. A standard and elegant trick is to instead maximize the logarithm of this quantity — a transformation that preserves the argmax while turning the exponential into a polynomial.

Since $\log$ is monotonically increasing on positive reals, maximizing $\log[\pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x})]$ over $c$ yields the same argmax as maximizing $\pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x})$. Let us compute this log explicitly.

7.2.1 The Log-Posterior and the Quadratic Discriminant Function

Substituting the Gaussian PDF into the log-numerator and ignoring the normalizing constant $(2\pi)^{d/2}$ (which does not depend on $c$ and therefore cannot affect the argmax), we obtain the quadratic discriminant function.

Definition · Quadratic Discriminant Function

For class $c$ in the GDA model, the quadratic discriminant function is $$q_c(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \log\!\left[\pi_c \cdot \frac{1}{\sigma_c^d} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2}{2\sigma_c^2}\right)\right] = \log\pi_c - d\log\sigma_c - \frac{\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2}{2\sigma_c^2}.$$ Note: we absorb the constant $-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi)$ into the normalizing constant we discard, since it is the same for every class.

The key structural observation is that $q_c(\mathbf{x})$ is a quadratic function of $\mathbf{x}$. Expanding the squared norm:

$$q_c(\mathbf{x}) = \log\pi_c - d\log\sigma_c - \frac{1}{2\sigma_c^2}\left(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x} - 2\boldsymbol\mu_c^\top\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol\mu_c^\top\boldsymbol\mu_c\right).$$

The term $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}$ is quadratic in $\mathbf{x}$; the term $\boldsymbol\mu_c^\top\mathbf{x}$ is linear; and all remaining terms ($\log\pi_c$, $d\log\sigma_c$, $\boldsymbol\mu_c^\top\boldsymbol\mu_c$) are constants that do not depend on $\mathbf{x}$. Thus the exponential is gone, and we work entirely in the realm of polynomials.

QDA Discriminant Function
$$\boxed{q_c(\mathbf{x}) = \log\pi_c - d\log\sigma_c - \frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2}{2\sigma_c^2}}$$
Theorem · Bayes Optimality of QDA

Under the GDA model with class-conditional distributions $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu_c, \sigma_c^2\mathbf{I})$ and priors $\pi_c$, the classifier $$r^*(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c \in \{1,\ldots,K\}} q_c(\mathbf{x})$$ is the Bayes optimal classifier: it minimizes the probability of misclassification among all classifiers.

Proof

The Bayes optimal classifier predicts the class with maximum posterior probability: $r^*(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \mathbb{P}(Y=c \mid \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})$. Since the denominator $f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{c'}\pi_{c'}f_{c'}(\mathbf{x})$ is strictly positive and independent of $c$,

$$\operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \mathbb{P}(Y=c \mid \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x}).$$

Since $\pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $c$ (by assumption), and $\log$ is strictly increasing,

$$\operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \log[\pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x})] = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c q_c(\mathbf{x}),$$

where the last equality uses the definition of $q_c$ and the fact that the dropped constant $-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi)$ does not affect the argmax. □

Example · Two-Class QDA in One Dimension

Setup. Suppose $d = 1$, and we have two classes with $\mu_C = 1$, $\sigma_C = 1$, $\pi_C = 0.6$ and $\mu_D = 4$, $\sigma_D = 2$, $\pi_D = 0.4$.

Discriminant functions. Since $d=1$, $q_c(x) = \log\pi_c - \log\sigma_c - (x - \mu_c)^2/(2\sigma_c^2)$. Thus: $$q_C(x) = \log 0.6 - 0 - \tfrac{(x-1)^2}{2}, \qquad q_D(x) = \log 0.4 - \log 2 - \tfrac{(x-4)^2}{8}.$$

Decision boundary. Setting $q_C(x) = q_D(x)$ yields the quadratic equation: $$\log 0.6 - \tfrac{(x-1)^2}{2} = \log 0.4 - \log 2 - \tfrac{(x-4)^2}{8}.$$ Expanding and collecting terms in $x$ gives $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ for some constants $a,b,c$, which has at most two solutions — these are the decision boundaries in 1D.

Interpretation. Because the two classes have different variances ($\sigma_C \ne \sigma_D$), the decision boundary is genuinely quadratic: there can be two crossover points in 1D. The larger-variance class $D$ has a flatter, wider Gaussian, which can create a scenario where $D$ is preferred both at the far left and far right of the real line, while $C$ is preferred in the middle.

7.2.2 The QDA Decision Boundary

For a two-class problem with classes $C$ and $D$, define the QDA decision function as $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = q_C(\mathbf{x}) - q_D(\mathbf{x})$. The Bayes classifier predicts $C$ if $\delta(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ and $D$ if $\delta(\mathbf{x}) < 0$. The decision boundary is the set $\{\mathbf{x} : \delta(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}$.

Since both $q_C$ and $q_D$ are quadratic functions of $\mathbf{x}$, their difference $\delta$ is also quadratic. In $d = 1$, $\delta(x) = 0$ is a degree-2 polynomial equation with at most two real solutions: the boundary consists of at most two points. In higher dimensions, $\{\mathbf{x} : \delta(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}$ is a quadric surface — in $d = 2$ this is a conic section (ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola). This is why the method is called quadratic discriminant analysis.

Warning · Two Decision Boundaries in QDA

When the two class variances differ substantially, QDA in 1D can produce two decision boundaries. This means that a region in the middle of the feature space might be classified as $C$, while the two tails are classified as $D$ — even though $D$'s mean is off to one side. This is not a bug: it correctly captures that a high-variance class has appreciable density far from its mean. Failing to appreciate this can lead to subtle misinterpretations of QDA output.

Figure 7.2. Left: The quadratic discriminant functions $q_C(x)$ (blue) and $q_D(x)$ (red) for a 1D two-class problem with $\mu_C=1$, $\sigma_C=1.2$, $\pi_C=0.55$ and $\mu_D=5.5$, $\sigma_D=1.6$, $\pi_D=0.45$. Both are concave parabolas. The golden dashed line marks the decision boundary where $q_C = q_D$. Note that the decision boundary is in the same position as in Figure 7.1 — taking the log has not moved the boundary, only changed the shape of the functions. Right: QDA decision regions in 2D. The blue region is classified as $C$ and the pink region as $D$; the gold curve is the elliptic decision boundary.
Data Science Application · QDA for Digit Recognition

In the MNIST handwritten digit classification task, we wish to distinguish among 10 classes ($K = 10$). Under QDA, we fit a Gaussian to the pixel vectors of each digit class, obtaining 10 mean vectors $\boldsymbol\mu_0, \ldots, \boldsymbol\mu_9$ (each of dimension $d = 784$) and 10 scalar variances $\sigma_0^2, \ldots, \sigma_9^2$. To classify a new image $\mathbf{x}$, we evaluate all 10 discriminant functions $q_0(\mathbf{x}), \ldots, q_9(\mathbf{x})$ and output the digit with the highest score. The computational cost is $O(Kd)$ per prediction — linear in both the number of classes and the feature dimension — making QDA highly scalable.

7.3 The Logistic Function as Posterior Probability

The QDA classifier outputs a discrete prediction: it tells us the most likely class for a given point $\mathbf{x}$. But in many applications we want more than a label — we want a confidence score, or more precisely, the probability that our prediction is correct. This section derives that posterior probability and reveals that it takes a remarkably elegant form: the logistic function, also known as the sigmoid.

The connection between Gaussian models and the sigmoid is not merely a mathematical curiosity. It is the conceptual bridge between GDA and logistic regression — two models that produce identical predictions under the GDA assumptions, but whose derivations and practical usage differ in important ways. Understanding this bridge gives us a deep insight into why the sigmoid appears pervasively throughout machine learning.

7.3.1 Deriving the Sigmoid from Bayes' Theorem

Consider the two-class case ($C$ and $D$). By Bayes' theorem, the posterior probability of class $C$ at a point $\mathbf{x}$ is:

$$\mathbb{P}(Y = C \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\pi_C f_C(\mathbf{x})}{\pi_C f_C(\mathbf{x}) + \pi_D f_D(\mathbf{x})}.$$

Recall that $q_c(\mathbf{x}) = \log[\pi_c \cdot \sigma_c^{-d} \cdot \exp(-\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2 / 2\sigma_c^2)]$, so equivalently $\pi_c \sigma_c^{-d} f_c(\mathbf{x}) \cdot (2\pi)^{d/2} = e^{q_c(\mathbf{x})}$. Factoring out the common constant $(2\pi)^{d/2}$:

$$\mathbb{P}(Y=C \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{q_C(\mathbf{x})}}{e^{q_C(\mathbf{x})} + e^{q_D(\mathbf{x})}}.$$

Dividing numerator and denominator by $e^{q_C(\mathbf{x})}$:

$$\mathbb{P}(Y=C \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{q_D(\mathbf{x}) - q_C(\mathbf{x})}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\delta(\mathbf{x})}},$$

where $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = q_C(\mathbf{x}) - q_D(\mathbf{x})$ is the QDA decision function. This final expression is the logistic function evaluated at the decision function.

Definition · The Logistic (Sigmoid) Function

The logistic function (also called the sigmoid function) is the map $s : \mathbb{R} \to (0, 1)$ defined by $$s(\gamma) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\gamma}}.$$ Key properties: $s(0) = 1/2$; $s$ is strictly monotonically increasing; $\lim_{\gamma \to +\infty} s(\gamma) = 1$; $\lim_{\gamma \to -\infty} s(\gamma) = 0$; and $s(-\gamma) = 1 - s(\gamma)$ (symmetry about $(0, 1/2)$).

Theorem · Posterior as Logistic Function of Decision Score

Under the two-class GDA model, the posterior probability of class $C$ satisfies $$\mathbb{P}(Y = C \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) = s\!\bigl(\delta(\mathbf{x})\bigr) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(q_C(\mathbf{x}) - q_D(\mathbf{x}))}},$$ where $s$ is the logistic function and $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = q_C(\mathbf{x}) - q_D(\mathbf{x})$ is the QDA decision function. In particular, $\mathbb{P}(Y=C \mid \mathbf{x}) > 1/2$ if and only if $\delta(\mathbf{x}) > 0$, confirming that the sign of $\delta$ determines the Bayes prediction.

Proof

From Bayes' theorem and the substitution $\pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x}) \propto e^{q_c(\mathbf{x})}$ established above: $$\mathbb{P}(Y=C \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{q_C}}{e^{q_C}+e^{q_D}} = \frac{1}{1+e^{q_D-q_C}} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-\delta(\mathbf{x})}} = s(\delta(\mathbf{x})).$$ The equivalence $s(\gamma) > 1/2 \iff \gamma > 0$ follows from $s$ being strictly increasing with $s(0)=1/2$. □

7.3.2 Interpreting the Sigmoid Output

The sigmoid's behavior has a direct and intuitive probabilistic interpretation. When $\mathbf{x}$ lies exactly on the decision boundary — that is, $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ — the posterior probability is exactly $1/2$: the two classes are equally likely. Moving away from the boundary in the direction of class $C$ increases $\delta(\mathbf{x})$, pushing the posterior toward 1. Moving away in the direction of class $D$ decreases $\delta(\mathbf{x})$, pushing the posterior toward 0. Far from the boundary, the classifier is highly confident; near the boundary, it is uncertain.

Figure 7.4. Left: The logistic function $s(\gamma) = 1/(1 + e^{-\gamma})$ as a function of the decision score $\gamma = q_C(x) - q_D(x)$. The function is 0.5 at $\gamma = 0$ (decision boundary, gold dashed), approaches 1 asymptotically for large positive $\gamma$, and approaches 0 for large negative $\gamma$. Blue fill indicates the $C$-preferred region; red fill indicates the $D$-preferred region. Right: The posterior $\mathbb{P}(Y=C \mid \mathbf{x})$ displayed as a heat map over the 2D feature space for an LDA model (shared variance). The gold line is the 0.5 iso-contour (the decision boundary), where the two classes are equally likely. The posterior varies only in the direction perpendicular to the decision boundary, explaining the 1D sweeping structure described in the lecture.
Example · Posterior Probability at a Test Point

Setup. Suppose in 1D we have $\mu_C = 0$, $\sigma_C = 1$, $\pi_C = 0.7$ and $\mu_D = 4$, $\sigma_D = 1$, $\pi_D = 0.3$, and we observe $x = 1.5$.

Compute discriminant functions. $$q_C(1.5) = \log(0.7) - \frac{(1.5-0)^2}{2} = -0.357 - 1.125 = -1.482.$$ $$q_D(1.5) = \log(0.3) - \frac{(1.5-4)^2}{2} = -1.204 - 3.125 = -4.329.$$

Decision score and posterior. $\delta(1.5) = q_C - q_D = -1.482 - (-4.329) = 2.847$. Thus $$\mathbb{P}(Y=C \mid x=1.5) = s(2.847) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-2.847}} \approx \frac{1}{1+0.058} \approx 0.945.$$

Interpretation. The classifier predicts class $C$ with 94.5% confidence. Even though $x = 1.5$ is somewhat between the two means, the strong prior $\pi_C = 0.7$ in favor of class $C$ and the shorter distance from $\mu_C = 0$ together produce high confidence in the $C$ prediction.

Intuition · The Sigmoid as a "Soft" Decision Boundary

The sign of $\delta(\mathbf{x})$ gives a hard classification: $C$ or $D$, nothing in between. The sigmoid $s(\delta(\mathbf{x}))$ gives a soft version: a smooth probability that varies continuously from 0 to 1 across the input space. Points deep inside one class region have posterior probabilities near 0 or 1; points near the boundary have posteriors near 0.5. This is precisely the information a downstream decision-maker needs to incorporate the classifier's uncertainty — for example, in settings where misclassification costs are asymmetric.

🔗
Connection to Logistic Regression: Logistic regression (Section 9.x) directly models the posterior as $\mathbb{P}(Y=C \mid \mathbf{x}) = s(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + \alpha)$ without assuming Gaussians. Under GDA with shared variance (LDA), the posterior happens to take exactly that form — so LDA and logistic regression predict the same probabilities when the LDA assumption holds. When it doesn't, logistic regression's flexibility is advantageous.

7.4 Linear Discriminant Analysis

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis is a powerful classifier, but its quadratic decision boundaries come at a cost: the shape of the boundary depends on the estimated variances $\hat{\sigma}_c^2$, which may be poorly estimated when training data is scarce. Furthermore, QDA has more parameters to estimate: both a mean $\boldsymbol\mu_c$ and a variance $\sigma_c^2$ per class. A natural regularization is to assume that all classes share the same variance, $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \cdots = \sigma_K^2 = \sigma^2$. Under this assumption, the quadratic terms in the QDA decision function cancel, yielding a linear decision function — the signature property of Linear Discriminant Analysis.

The equal-variance assumption may seem restrictive, but it is often a reasonable approximation. When the features are normalized, or when the classes really do have similar spreads, LDA can outperform QDA by virtue of lower variance in the parameter estimates. As always, model selection between LDA and QDA should be guided by cross-validation.

7.4.1 The Equal-Variance Assumption and Linear Simplification

Assume $\sigma_C^2 = \sigma_D^2 = \sigma^2$. The QDA decision function becomes:

$$\delta(\mathbf{x}) = q_C(\mathbf{x}) - q_D(\mathbf{x}) = \left(\log\pi_C - d\log\sigma - \frac{\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) - \left(\log\pi_D - d\log\sigma - \frac{\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$

The terms $d\log\sigma$ cancel immediately. Expanding the squared norms:

$$\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2 - \|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2 = (\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x} - 2\boldsymbol\mu_C^\top\mathbf{x} + \|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2) - (\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x} - 2\boldsymbol\mu_D^\top\mathbf{x} + \|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2).$$

The $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}$ terms cancel (this is the key step!), leaving:

$$\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{2(\boldsymbol\mu_C - \boldsymbol\mu_D)^\top\mathbf{x} - \|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2 + \|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log\frac{\pi_C}{\pi_D}.$$

This is linear in $\mathbf{x}$.

Definition · LDA Decision Function

Under the GDA model with shared variance $\sigma^2$, the LDA decision function for two classes $C$ and $D$ is $$\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + \alpha,$$ where the weight vector and bias are $$\mathbf{w} = \frac{\boldsymbol\mu_C - \boldsymbol\mu_D}{\sigma^2}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log\frac{\pi_C}{\pi_D}.$$ The Bayes classifier predicts $C$ if $\delta(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ and $D$ otherwise. The decision boundary $\{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + \alpha = 0\}$ is a hyperplane.

LDA Weight Vector
$$\mathbf{w} = \frac{\boldsymbol\mu_C - \boldsymbol\mu_D}{\sigma^2}$$

The weight vector $\mathbf{w} = (\boldsymbol\mu_C - \boldsymbol\mu_D)/\sigma^2$ is proportional to the vector pointing from the mean of $D$ to the mean of $C$. Geometrically, the decision boundary is the hyperplane perpendicular to this vector, displaced from the midpoint of $\boldsymbol\mu_C$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_D$ by the amount $\alpha$ (which corrects for unequal priors). When $\pi_C = \pi_D$, the $\log(\pi_C/\pi_D)$ term vanishes and the boundary passes through the midpoint of the two class means — this is exactly the centroid classifier from Chapter 2.

Theorem · LDA Recovers the Centroid Classifier Under Equal Priors

If $\pi_C = \pi_D = 1/2$ and both classes have the same variance $\sigma^2$, the LDA decision boundary is the hyperplane that perpendicularly bisects the line segment $[\boldsymbol\mu_C, \boldsymbol\mu_D]$. In particular, this is the set $$\left\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d : \left(\boldsymbol\mu_C - \boldsymbol\mu_D\right)^\top\!\mathbf{x} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2\right)\right\}.$$

Proof

Setting $\pi_C = \pi_D$ makes $\log(\pi_C/\pi_D) = 0$, so $\alpha = (\|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2)/(2\sigma^2)$. The decision boundary $\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + \alpha = 0$ becomes $$\frac{(\boldsymbol\mu_C - \boldsymbol\mu_D)^\top\mathbf{x}}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2}{2\sigma^2} = 0,$$ which simplifies to $(\boldsymbol\mu_C-\boldsymbol\mu_D)^\top\mathbf{x} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2)$. The midpoint $\mathbf{m} = (\boldsymbol\mu_C+\boldsymbol\mu_D)/2$ satisfies this: $(\boldsymbol\mu_C-\boldsymbol\mu_D)^\top\mathbf{m} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\|\boldsymbol\mu_C\|^2-\|\boldsymbol\mu_D\|^2)$, confirming the midpoint lies on the boundary. The boundary is perpendicular to $\boldsymbol\mu_C-\boldsymbol\mu_D$ by the form of the equation. □

Figure 7.3. Comparison of QDA (left) and LDA (right) decision boundaries for a two-class problem with class means $\boldsymbol\mu_C = (0,0)$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_D = (5,4)$. Left (QDA): The two classes have different variances ($\sigma_C^2 = 1$, $\sigma_D^2 = 3$), so the decision boundary (gold curve) is a conic section — here a curved boundary that is not a straight line. Right (LDA): Both classes share the variance $\sigma^2 = 2$; the quadratic terms cancel and the decision boundary becomes a straight line (hyperplane) that perpendicularly bisects the segment between the class means (since equal priors are used). The contrast highlights how the equal-variance assumption fundamentally changes the geometry of the classifier.

7.4.2 Multi-Class LDA and the Voronoi Connection

The LDA framework extends naturally to $K > 2$ classes. For each class $c$, define its linear discriminant function:

$$\ell_c(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\boldsymbol\mu_c^\top\mathbf{x}}{\sigma^2} - \frac{\|\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log\pi_c.$$

Under the equal-variance assumption, the multi-class Bayes rule is $r^*(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \ell_c(\mathbf{x})$. This can be derived by noting that $q_c(\mathbf{x}) = \ell_c(\mathbf{x}) + \text{const}$ where the constant is the same for all classes (it involves only $\sigma$ and $d$, not $c$).

Definition · Multi-Class Linear Discriminant Function

In the $K$-class LDA model with shared variance $\sigma^2$, the linear discriminant function} for class $c$ is $$\ell_c(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\boldsymbol\mu_c^\top\mathbf{x}}{\sigma^2} - \frac{\|\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log\pi_c.$$ The multi-class LDA classifier predicts $r^*(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c=1}^K \ell_c(\mathbf{x})$.

When all priors are equal ($\pi_c = 1/K$ for all $c$), the log-prior terms vanish and $\ell_c(\mathbf{x}) \propto \boldsymbol\mu_c^\top\mathbf{x} - \|\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2/2$. This is equivalent to choosing the class $c$ that minimizes $\|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2$ — i.e., the nearest centroid. The resulting decision regions are standard Voronoi cells, with straight (hyperplanar) boundaries equidistant between adjacent class means. With unequal priors, the boundaries shift to give larger regions to more probable classes, yielding an additively weighted Voronoi diagram.

Intuition · LDA as Nearest Centroid Under Equal Priors

When all classes have equal prior probability and equal variance, LDA reduces to: "find the class whose mean is closest to the test point, in Euclidean distance." The hyperplanar decision boundaries are exactly the perpendicular bisectors of the segments joining adjacent class means. This is the simplest possible generative classifier — and it is the Bayes optimal one under these symmetry conditions. When priors differ, LDA shifts each boundary toward the less probable class, effectively "shrinking" the decision region of rare classes.

Figure 7.5. Multi-class decision regions for 6 classes (colored dots = class means, colored regions = decision cells) under QDA (left) and LDA (right) with equal priors. Left (QDA): Each class has its own variance; the decision boundaries are curved quadric surfaces. The cells are irregularly shaped, with larger-variance classes claiming more area. Right (LDA): All classes share the same variance; the decision boundaries are straight lines forming a cell complex — a true Voronoi diagram of the class means. The contrast illustrates why LDA is often described as a weighted nearest-centroid classifier.
Data Science Application · LDA for Face Recognition

In Eigenface-based face recognition, each person's face images are modeled as a Gaussian cluster in a high-dimensional pixel (or PCA-reduced) space. LDA provides an optimal linear classifier: compute $\ell_c(\mathbf{x})$ for each person $c$ and return the identity with the highest score. The key computational advantage over full covariance models is that LDA requires estimating only $K$ mean vectors (and one shared variance), making it tractable even when $d$ (the number of face pixels or PCA components) is large relative to the number of training images per person.

7.5 Maximum Likelihood Estimation

So far we have assumed that the parameters of the GDA model — the class means $\boldsymbol\mu_c$, variances $\sigma_c^2$, and priors $\pi_c$ — are known. In practice, of course, they must be estimated from training data. The standard and principled framework for doing so is Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), invented by R. A. Fisher around 1912 and arguably the most important idea in classical statistics.

The core idea of MLE is elegantly simple: among all possible values of the parameter $\theta$, choose the value that makes the observed data most probable. This requires us to define, and then maximize, a function called the likelihood. We begin with a discrete example — estimating the bias of a coin — to build intuition, then extend to the continuous Gaussian case that directly applies to GDA.

7.5.1 The Likelihood Function and MLE Formulation

Suppose we flip a (possibly biased) coin $n$ times and observe $x$ heads. The number of heads follows a Binomial distribution: $X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)$, with PMF

$$\mathbb{P}(X = x \mid p) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}.$$

This expression is normally read as a function of the data $x$ given a fixed parameter $p$. The MLE perspective inverts this: we observe a fixed outcome $x = 8$ out of $n = 10$ flips, and we ask: for which value of $p$ is this outcome most probable?

Definition · Likelihood Function

Given observed data $x$ generated from a parametric model $\mathbb{P}(X = x \mid \theta)$ (or density $f(x;\theta)$ for continuous data), the likelihood function is $$\mathcal{L}(\theta) \triangleq \mathbb{P}(X = x \mid \theta) \quad \text{(viewed as a function of } \theta \text{, with } x \text{ fixed)}.$$ The log-likelihood is $\ell(\theta) \triangleq \log \mathcal{L}(\theta)$. The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) is $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_\theta \ell(\theta).$$

For the coin example with $x = 8, n = 10$: $\mathcal{L}(p) = \binom{10}{8} p^8 (1-p)^2$. To find the maximum, we differentiate the log-likelihood $\ell(p) = \log\binom{10}{8} + 8\log p + 2\log(1-p)$ with respect to $p$, set to zero:

$$\frac{d\ell}{dp} = \frac{8}{p} - \frac{2}{1-p} = 0 \implies \hat{p} = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8.$$

The MLE is exactly the observed frequency — a reassuring sanity check. More generally, for Binomial data, $\hat{p}_{\text{MLE}} = x/n$.

Theorem · MLE for Binomial Parameter

Let $X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)$ and suppose we observe $X = x$. The maximum likelihood estimator of $p$ is $$\hat{p}_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{x}{n},$$ the sample proportion of successes. It is an unbiased estimator of $p$: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{p}] = p$.

Proof

We maximize $\ell(p) = x\log p + (n-x)\log(1-p)$ (the binomial coefficient is a constant). Setting $d\ell/dp = x/p - (n-x)/(1-p) = 0$ gives $x(1-p) = (n-x)p$, hence $x = np$, so $\hat{p} = x/n$. The second derivative $-x/p^2 - (n-x)/(1-p)^2 < 0$ confirms it is a maximum. Unbiasedness: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{p}] = \mathbb{E}[X]/n = np/n = p$. □

Figure 7.6. Likelihood (left) and log-likelihood (right) for a Binomial model with $n=10$ flips and $x=8$ observed heads, as functions of the bias parameter $p \in (0,1)$. Both functions achieve their maximum at $\hat{p} = 0.8$ (red dashed line), confirming the MLE formula $\hat{p} = x/n$. The log-likelihood (right) is a strictly concave function of $p$, making the maximum unique and the optimization well-behaved. The two functions have identical argmax because $\log$ is a monotone transformation.

7.5.2 MLE for Gaussian Parameters

Now consider the case directly relevant to GDA: estimating the parameters $\boldsymbol\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ of a multivariate Gaussian from $n$ i.i.d. observations $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu, \sigma^2\mathbf{I})$. The joint log-likelihood is:

$$\ell(\boldsymbol\mu, \sigma^2) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(\mathbf{x}_i; \boldsymbol\mu, \sigma^2) = -\frac{nd}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{nd}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol\mu\|^2.$$
Theorem · MLE for Isotropic Gaussian Parameters

Given $n$ i.i.d. observations $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n$ from $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu, \sigma^2\mathbf{I})$, the MLE estimators are: $$\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{\text{MLE}} = \bar{\mathbf{x}} \triangleq \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{x}_i \qquad \text{(sample mean)},$$ $$\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{nd}\sum_{i=1}^n \|\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu}\|^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}}\|^2}{d} \qquad \text{(biased sample variance)}.$$

Proof

For $\boldsymbol\mu$: The log-likelihood depends on $\boldsymbol\mu$ only through $-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i\|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol\mu\|^2$. Minimizing this sum of squared distances over $\boldsymbol\mu$ gives the sample mean: $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\mu}\sum_i\|\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|^2 = -2\sum_i(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu) = 0 \implies \hat{\boldsymbol\mu} = \bar{\mathbf{x}}$.

For $\sigma^2$: Substituting $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu} = \bar{\mathbf{x}}$, the log-likelihood becomes a function of $\sigma^2$ only. Let $S = \sum_i\|\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\|^2$. Then $\ell = -\frac{nd}{2}\log\sigma^2 - \frac{S}{2\sigma^2} + \text{const}$. Setting $d\ell/d(\sigma^2) = -\frac{nd}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{S}{2(\sigma^2)^2} = 0$ gives $\hat{\sigma}^2 = S/(nd)$. □

Warning · The MLE Variance Estimator is Biased

The MLE variance $\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}} = S/(nd)$ systematically underestimates the true variance: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{MLE}}] = \sigma^2(n-1)/n < \sigma^2$. The standard unbiased estimator corrects for this by dividing by $n-1$ instead of $n$: $s^2 = S/(d(n-1))$. For large $n$ the difference is negligible, but for small datasets the bias can be meaningful. In GDA, practitioners often use the unbiased estimator in practice, though the theoretical analysis of GDA uses the MLE.

For GDA, we apply this MLE procedure separately to the training data in each class. Let $n_c$ denote the number of training points in class $c$, and let $\mathcal{C}_c = \{i : y_i = c\}$. Then:

GDA Parameter Estimates
$$\hat{\pi}_c = \frac{n_c}{n}, \qquad \hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_c = \frac{1}{n_c}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}_c}\mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \hat{\sigma}^2_c = \frac{1}{n_c d}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}_c}\|\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_c\|^2.$$
Example · Fitting a GDA Model to Training Data

Setup. We have $n = 20$ training points in $d = 2$ dimensions: 12 from class $C$ and 8 from class $D$. The class $C$ points have sample mean $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_C = (1.2, 0.8)^\top$ and average squared deviation $\sum_{i \in C}\|\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_C\|^2 = 24$. Class $D$ has $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_D = (4.5, 3.2)^\top$ and $\sum_{i \in D}\|\mathbf{x}_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_D\|^2 = 32$.

Estimates. $$\hat{\pi}_C = 12/20 = 0.6, \quad \hat{\pi}_D = 8/20 = 0.4.$$ $$\hat{\sigma}_C^2 = \frac{24}{12 \cdot 2} = 1.0, \quad \hat{\sigma}_D^2 = \frac{32}{8 \cdot 2} = 2.0.$$

Classification.} With these estimates, we compute $q_C(\mathbf{x})$ and $q_D(\mathbf{x})$ for any test point and apply the QDA decision rule. For LDA, we would use a pooled variance estimate: $\hat{\sigma}^2 = (24 + 32)/((12+8)\cdot 2) = 56/40 = 1.4$.

Figure 7.7. MLE for a 1D Gaussian with true parameters $\mu = 3.0$, $\sigma = 1.5$, and $n = 30$ samples. Left: Histogram of the 30 data points, with the true distribution (red dashed) and the MLE fit $\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mu}, \hat{\sigma}^2)$ (blue solid) overlaid. The MLE fit closely tracks the true distribution, with slight deviations due to finite sample variability. Right: Log-likelihood surface $\ell(\mu, \sigma)$ as a function of both parameters simultaneously. The gold star marks the MLE $(\hat{\mu}, \hat{\sigma})$ at the maximum; the red dot marks the true parameter values. The surface is strictly concave (bowl-shaped), guaranteeing a unique global maximum.
Data Science Application · MLE for Prior Probability Estimation

Estimating class priors $\pi_c$ is one of the most practically consequential steps in GDA. The MLE estimate $\hat{\pi}_c = n_c/n$ is correct when the training data is an unbiased sample of the population. In many real applications — such as fraud detection, medical diagnosis, or rare-event prediction — the training data is oversampled for the rare class to ensure enough examples for learning. In such cases, the empirical class frequencies do not reflect the true population priors, and using $\hat{\pi}_c = n_c/n$ will give a miscalibrated classifier. Practitioners must either correct the priors using domain knowledge or use calibration methods to adjust the posterior probabilities.

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter developed Gaussian Discriminant Analysis from first principles, tracing the complete path from probabilistic assumptions to a concrete, computable classifier. We began by modeling each class as a multivariate Gaussian with scalar variance (isotropic spread), which makes the class-conditional density a function of Euclidean distance from the class mean. Applying the Bayes decision rule — predict the class with highest posterior probability — we derived the quadratic discriminant function $q_c(\mathbf{x})$ by taking the log of the numerator of Bayes' theorem, revealing that the exponential vanishes and the decision function is a quadratic in $\mathbf{x}$. The resulting classifier is QDA.

A crucial structural result is that the posterior probability takes the form of the logistic (sigmoid) function applied to the decision score $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = q_C - q_D$. This connects GDA to logistic regression and neural networks, where the sigmoid appears as the natural transformation from a linear score to a probability. Imposing the additional constraint that all classes share the same variance $\sigma^2$ cancels the quadratic terms in $\delta$, giving the linear decision function of LDA. Under equal priors, LDA reduces to the centroid classifier (nearest-mean), and the decision regions become standard Voronoi cells. Finally, we studied Maximum Likelihood Estimation — the principled method for fitting the Gaussian parameters from data — deriving the sample mean and (biased) sample variance as MLEs for $\boldsymbol\mu$ and $\sigma^2$.

GDA GENERATIVE MODEL

Each class $c$ generates data via $\mathbf{X}|Y=c \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu_c, \sigma_c^2\mathbf{I})$ with prior $\pi_c$. The joint model $f(\mathbf{x},c) = \pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x})$ encodes full distributional knowledge of the data. Classifying reduces to comparing posterior probabilities $\mathbb{P}(Y=c|\mathbf{x}) \propto \pi_c f_c(\mathbf{x})$.

ISOTROPIC GAUSSIAN

The density $f(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\mu,\sigma^2) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu\|^2/(2\sigma^2))$ has spherical iso-contours because the variance $\sigma^2$ is the same in every direction. This simplification reduces the number of parameters per class from $O(d^2)$ to $O(d)$, trading expressiveness for tractability.

QDA DISCRIMINANT FUNCTION

Taking the log-numerator of the posterior gives $q_c(\mathbf{x}) = \log\pi_c - d\log\sigma_c - \|\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu_c\|^2/(2\sigma_c^2)$, which is quadratic in $\mathbf{x}$. The Bayes classifier is $r^*(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{arg\,max}_c q_c(\mathbf{x})$. The decision boundary $\{q_C = q_D\}$ is a quadric surface.

LOGISTIC (SIGMOID) FUNCTION

The posterior probability of class $C$ equals $s(\delta(\mathbf{x})) = 1/(1+e^{-\delta(\mathbf{x})})$ where $\delta = q_C - q_D$ is the decision function. The sigmoid maps $(-\infty,+\infty) \to (0,1)$, is 0.5 at the decision boundary, and approaches 1 (resp. 0) deep in the $C$ (resp. $D$) region. It is the bridge between GDA and logistic regression.

LDA: EQUAL-VARIANCE ASSUMPTION

When $\sigma_c^2 = \sigma^2$ for all $c$, the quadratic $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}$ terms cancel in $q_C - q_D$, yielding the linear decision function $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + \alpha$ with $\mathbf{w} = (\boldsymbol\mu_C-\boldsymbol\mu_D)/\sigma^2$. The decision boundary is a hyperplane perpendicular to the vector between class means.

LDA AS NEAREST CENTROID

Under equal priors and equal variances, LDA is equivalent to predicting the class with the nearest mean in Euclidean distance. The resulting decision regions form a Voronoi diagram of the class means. Unequal priors shift boundaries toward less probable classes, giving a weighted Voronoi diagram.

MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATION

The MLE chooses parameters $\hat{\theta} = \operatorname{arg\,max}_\theta \ell(\theta)$ where $\ell(\theta) = \log\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ is the log-likelihood. Maximizing the log-likelihood is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood because $\log$ is monotone. For i.i.d. data, the log-likelihood decomposes into a sum over observations, making optimization tractable.

MLE FOR GAUSSIAN PARAMETERS

Given $n$ i.i.d. samples from $\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\mu,\sigma^2\mathbf{I})$, the MLEs are $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu} = \bar{\mathbf{x}}$ (sample mean) and $\hat{\sigma}^2 = \sum_i\|\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\|^2/(nd)$ (biased sample variance). The bias $(n-1)/n$ can be corrected by dividing by $n-1$ instead of $n$, yielding the unbiased estimator $s^2$.

GDA PARAMETER ESTIMATION

In practice, fit GDA by estimating class priors as $\hat{\pi}_c = n_c/n$, class means as $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_c = \bar{\mathbf{x}}_c$, and class variances as the within-class MLE variance. For LDA, pool the variance across classes: $\hat{\sigma}^2 = \sum_c\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_c}\|\mathbf{x}_i-\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_c\|^2/(nd)$.

MODEL SELECTION: LDA VS QDA

LDA has fewer parameters and lower variance, making it preferable when training data is limited or the equal-variance assumption approximately holds. QDA is more flexible but requires more data to estimate reliably. Cross-validation is the reliable arbiter. Typically, LDA is preferred when $n$ is small relative to $d$.

Exercises

Exercise 7.1  ·  QDA DERIVATION
Deriving the QDA Decision Boundary for Medical Diagnosis

Consider a binary disease screening task ($d=1$) where healthy patients ($C$) have $\mu_C = 10$, $\sigma_C = 2$ and diseased patients ($D$) have $\mu_D = 16$, $\sigma_D = 4$, with priors $\pi_C = 0.9$ and $\pi_D = 0.1$.

  1. (Derivation) Write out the quadratic discriminant functions $q_C(x)$ and $q_D(x)$ explicitly. Show that the decision function $\delta(x) = q_C(x) - q_D(x)$ is a quadratic polynomial in $x$, identify its coefficients, and find all decision boundaries by solving $\delta(x) = 0$.
  2. (Computation) For test values $x \in \{8, 12, 16, 20\}$, compute $q_C(x)$, $q_D(x)$, and the predicted class. Are there any values of $x$ where the prediction is perhaps counterintuitive (e.g., $D$ predicted for small $x$)?
  3. (Interpretation) Explain in words why QDA can produce two decision boundaries in 1D. Under what conditions on $\sigma_C$ and $\sigma_D$ does QDA reduce to LDA (single linear boundary)? What happens to the number of boundaries as $\sigma_D/\sigma_C \to \infty$?
  4. (Data Science) A hospital uses this model for triaging. Compute the posterior probability $\mathbb{P}(Y=D \mid x = 18)$ using the logistic formula from Section 7.3. How does the asymmetric loss of missing a disease case (false negative) change the optimal decision threshold, and which term in $\delta(x)$ should be modified?
Exercise 7.2  ·  SIGMOID PROPERTIES
The Logistic Function in Neural Network Output Layers

The sigmoid $s(\gamma) = 1/(1+e^{-\gamma})$ is the canonical output activation for binary classification in neural networks. Understanding its properties is essential.

  1. (Derivation) Prove that $s'(\gamma) = s(\gamma)(1-s(\gamma))$. This identity is crucial for backpropagation. Then derive a closed-form expression for $s''(\gamma)$ and show that $s''(\gamma) = 0$ at $\gamma = \ln(\sqrt{3} \pm 1)$ (the inflection points).
  2. (Computation) Compute $s(0)$, $s(1)$, $s(-1)$, $s(5)$, $s(-5)$. For what value of $\gamma$ does $s(\gamma) = 0.9$? Explain the relationship $s(-\gamma) = 1 - s(\gamma)$ geometrically.
  3. (Interpretation) In the GDA context, the posterior $\mathbb{P}(Y=C|\mathbf{x}) = s(\delta(\mathbf{x}))$. Explain why a prediction is "certain" (posterior near 0 or 1) far from the decision boundary, and "uncertain" (posterior near 0.5) close to the boundary. How does this property make the sigmoid useful as a probability output?
  4. (Extension) The softmax function generalizes the sigmoid to $K$ classes: $\text{softmax}(\mathbf{q})_c = e^{q_c}/\sum_{c'}e^{q_{c'}}$. Show that for $K=2$, $\text{softmax}((q_C, q_D))_C = s(q_C - q_D)$. This connects multi-class GDA to multi-class logistic regression.
Exercise 7.3  ·  LDA GEOMETRY
Linear Discriminant Analysis for Sentiment Classification

A text classifier uses two TF-IDF features ($d=2$) to distinguish positive ($C$) and negative ($D$) reviews. Assume $\boldsymbol\mu_C = (3, 1)^\top$, $\boldsymbol\mu_D = (1, 3)^\top$, shared $\sigma^2 = 2$, and equal priors.

  1. (Derivation) Derive the LDA weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ and bias $\alpha$ using the formulas from Section 7.4. Write the equation of the decision boundary as a line $w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \alpha = 0$. Show that this line passes through the midpoint $\mathbf{m} = (\boldsymbol\mu_C+\boldsymbol\mu_D)/2$ and is perpendicular to $\boldsymbol\mu_C - \boldsymbol\mu_D$.
  2. (Computation) Classify the test points $\mathbf{x}_1 = (2, 2)^\top$, $\mathbf{x}_2 = (4, 0)^\top$, $\mathbf{x}_3 = (0, 4)^\top$, and $\mathbf{x}_4 = (1, 1)^\top$. For each, compute $\delta(\mathbf{x})$ and the posterior probability of class $C$.
  3. (Interpretation) Now suppose the priors change to $\pi_C = 0.8$ and $\pi_D = 0.2$ (positive reviews are 4× more common). Recompute $\alpha$ and describe how the decision boundary shifts. Which test points change their classification?
  4. (Data Science) Explain how LDA relates to Fisher's Linear Discriminant — a classical dimensionality reduction technique. In particular, if you projected all data onto the vector $\mathbf{w}$, how would the projected class distributions look, and why does this projection maximize the "separation" between classes?
Exercise 7.4  ·  MLE DERIVATION
Maximum Likelihood for Exponential Distribution in Network Traffic Modeling

Inter-arrival times of network packets are often modeled as Exponential: $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ with density $f(x;\lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \geq 0$. We observe i.i.d. samples $x_1, \ldots, x_n$.

  1. (Derivation) Write the log-likelihood $\ell(\lambda) = \log\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\lambda)$. Differentiate with respect to $\lambda$, set to zero, and derive the MLE $\hat{\lambda}_{\text{MLE}}$. Express the answer in terms of the sample mean $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i$.
  2. (Computation) You observe 5 inter-arrival times (in milliseconds): 2.1, 0.8, 3.4, 1.5, 2.2. Compute the MLE $\hat{\lambda}$ and the estimated mean inter-arrival time $1/\hat{\lambda}$.
  3. (Interpretation) Verify that the MLE satisfies a "plug-in" principle: $1/\hat{\lambda}$ equals the sample mean $\bar{x}$. Is this a coincidence, or is it a general property of the MLE for exponential families? What does this say about the MLE for the Gaussian mean?
  4. (Data Science) A network anomaly detector classifies high-traffic intervals (low $\lambda$) from normal intervals. If you model two states (normal: $\lambda_N$, attack: $\lambda_A$) with priors, how would you use GDA with Exponential (rather than Gaussian) class-conditionals? Derive the decision function $q_N(x) - q_A(x)$ and show it is linear in $x$. This is the principle behind naive Bayes with exponential features.
Exercise 7.5  ·  MULTI-CLASS GDA
Multi-Class QDA for Iris Species Classification

The classic Iris dataset has $K=3$ species and $d=2$ features (sepal length and width). Suppose we have fitted GDA and obtained: $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_1=(5.0,3.4)^\top$, $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_2=(5.9,2.8)^\top$, $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}_3=(6.6,3.0)^\top$, with $\hat{\sigma}_1^2=0.20$, $\hat{\sigma}_2^2=0.30$, $\hat{\sigma}_3^2=0.35$, and equal priors $\hat{\pi}_c = 1/3$.

  1. (Derivation) Write out the three QDA discriminant functions $q_1(\mathbf{x})$, $q_2(\mathbf{x})$, $q_3(\mathbf{x})$ explicitly using the given parameters. Verify that each is a quadratic function of $\mathbf{x}$.
  2. (Computation) Classify the test point $\mathbf{x} = (6.0, 3.0)^\top$ by evaluating $q_c(\mathbf{x})$ for all three classes. Which class is predicted? Compute the posterior probabilities using the softmax formula $\mathbb{P}(Y=c|\mathbf{x}) = e^{q_c(\mathbf{x})}/\sum_{c'}e^{q_{c'}(\mathbf{x})}$.
  3. (Interpretation) Now apply LDA instead (use a pooled variance $\hat{\sigma}^2 = (\hat{\sigma}_1^2+\hat{\sigma}_2^2+\hat{\sigma}_3^2)/3$). Write the three linear discriminant functions $\ell_c(\mathbf{x})$ and classify the same test point. Do the two methods agree? Explain geometrically why LDA might give a different answer when class variances differ.
  4. (Data Science) In a real GDA implementation, discuss how the softmax formula avoids numerical overflow when evaluating $e^{q_c(\mathbf{x})}$ for large values of the discriminant. The standard fix is to subtract $\max_c q_c(\mathbf{x})$ before exponentiating. Show algebraically that this does not change the softmax output, and explain why it is numerically essential in high-dimensional settings.
